evidence: createApp() builds Catalogue, OrderService and CatalogueService: composition root and wiring, an infrastructure job
app.get/post/patch handlers only read req params/body, call application services and write res.status().json(): HTTP transport adapter
POST /orders checks Array.isArray(items) && items.length > 0 and returns 400: checks request shape at the transport boundary
catch blocks turn Error.message into an HTTP 400 response: mapping errors to transport responses
catalogueService.addProduct('PROD001', ...) sample data: startup seeding through the application service, with no domain rules in this file
Order creation, state transitions and cancellation are handed to orderService.createOrder/transitionOrder/cancelOrder
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/infrastructure/app.ts does work that belongs in an infrastructure layer. It is the composition root: it creates Catalogue, OrderService and CatalogueService and wires them together. It sets up Express (JSON middleware and route handlers), maps HTTP requests to application service calls, and turns results and exceptions into HTTP status codes and JSON bodies. These are transport and framework jobs, which fit the infrastructure layer kind. No business logic is done here. Pricing, stock checks, order state transitions and cancellation rules are all handed to OrderService and CatalogueService. The checks in POST /orders (items must be a non-empty array) and PATCH /orders/:orderId/state (state must be present) only check the shape of the request at the transport boundary. The domain or application layer may still enforce the matching invariants. Seeding sample products through catalogueService.addProduct happens at startup and calls the application service. It does not put product rules in this file. The one borderline point is that 'items must not be empty' could also be read as a business invariant. Because it sits next to other request-shape checks and is answered with HTTP 400, I treat it as transport validation.
